Chapter 8, Akṣarabrahmayoga, "the yoga of the imperishable brahman," opens with Arjuna asking seven rapid questions left over from the close of chapter 7: what are brahman, the individual self, action, material existence, the divine order, and the lord of sacrifice, and how is Kṛṣṇa to be known at the moment of death? Kṛṣṇa answers the first six in two terse verses, identifying brahman with akṣara, "the imperishable," and defining each remaining term in turn, before turning to the seventh question, which occupies the rest of the chapter: what happens at death. His answer is that a person becomes, at death, whatever state of mind they have dwelt on throughout life, so that constant remembrance of Kṛṣṇa, sustained through the discipline of yoga, determines the outcome; several verses describe the yogic technique of dying consciously, fixing the breath between the eyebrows or at the crown of the head while uttering the sacred syllable Om. Kṛṣṇa then contrasts the fate of those who reach him, final release from rebirth, with even the highest heavens short of that goal, which remain subject to return, on a cosmic timescale measured in Brahmā's single day and night of a thousand ages each. The chapter closes by naming two paths a departed soul may take, one of fire, day and the sun's northern course leading to no return, the other of smoke, night and its southern course leading back to rebirth, and ends by declaring that the yogin who understands all this surpasses even the rewards of Vedic ritual and reaches the supreme, primal abode.
